source.title: Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests refusal steering with contrastive activation vectors and reports refusal behavior, but does not reproduce the original direction construction and intervention in full.
record.gate_note: The refusal experiment compares activation steering using refusal data with weight steering and other baselines. It does not test ablation of the original residual-stream direction, and it does not test refusal on harmless requests. Numerical values for the refusal results are shown only in figures.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on contrastive weight steering. Activation steering appears only as a baseline, built Chen et al. (persona vectors) style: mean activations over refusal responses minus mean activations over the model fed compliant answers, all on harmful queries. That is not V1's harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction. The study never ablates any direction, never tests refusal induction on harmless prompts, and never asks whether a single direction mediates refusal. The refusal experiment (Llama-2-7b-chat after GSM8K fine-tuning) compares methods for restoring safety. Its activation-baseline results concern a related but differently constructed vector, so they go under fits_no_version rather than testing V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that contrastive weight steering generalizes further than activation steering. In the refusal setting, weight steering with refusal data is as effective as joint training with refusal data and outperforms activation steering, while preserving GSM8K gains. They make no claim about the single-direction account.
record.recipe_differences: The refusal experiment uses contrastive activation and weight steering after GSM8K fine-tuning. Its activation data contrasts refusals with answers to harmful queries; it does not use the original harmful-versus-harmless instruction difference construction or ablate a direction.
record.method_sensitivity: For refusal restoration, single-layer and all-layer activation steering differ in effectiveness; the text says all-layer activation steering outperforms single-layer activation, while remaining substantially weaker than full weight steering.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a response-contrast refusal activation vector (single layer 17, or all layers) to Llama-2-7b-chat after GSM8K fine-tuning restores some safety on DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger. It is substantially weaker than contrastive weight steering, and the text gives no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Response-level refusal activation vectors restore eroded refusal after benign fine-tuning less effectively than weight-space steering.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastive weight steering with refuse-vs-answer data restores refusal after GSM8K fine-tuning while keeping GSM8K gains. It is about as effective as joint training with refusal examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A contrastive refusal weight vector can restore safety behavior after task-specific fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint fine-tuning with 5% added refusal examples restores safety.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding refusal examples during task fine-tuning preserves refusal.

record.problems: The refusal experiment uses one chat model and narrow safety datasets. The refusal outcomes are presented in figures without extractable numeric values in the text. The study does not test harmless-request refusals or the original direction's ablation.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported refusal results were omitted.

untested.parts: The harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, ablation removing refusal, addition inducing refusal on harmless prompts, and preservation of capabilities under that intervention.
Abliteration via weight orthogonalization. The weight steering here is a fine-tune-difference task vector, not direction removal.
All of it. The study shows fine-tuning erodes refusal but does not examine direction structure.

missing.what: Steering with the non-evil (evil-data) vector is ineffective for both activation and weight methods. The non-contrastive refusal task vector degrades GSM8K and does not improve safety. All-layer activation and bias-only weight steering beat single-layer activation but stay weaker than full weight steering.
Attack success rate results (unsafety score = 5) for all methods.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V1 limits_scope label is downgraded. The activation baseline follows Chen et al. (2025) persona vectors: refusal-response activations minus activations on fed-in harmful answers. It is selected at one layer and used only additively to restore refusal in a fine-tuned model. It is a comparator to the authors' method, not a test of the difference-in-means instruction direction. All refusal values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests steering toward refusal on harmful requests after GSM8K fine-tuning, using a contrastive activation vector. Does not test removing the original direction, the original harmful-minus-harmless instruction construction, refusal on harmless requests, or the full all-layer ablation claim.
Does not test abliteration or removal of refusal by a weight edit.
Does not test jailbreak suppression of the direction or training against its ablation.
Does not compare a single refusal direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not compare refusal-training schedules or establish when a removable direction exists.
